summary: Specifies a minimum set of requirements for Internet resource locators, which convey location and access information for resources. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of what an address for something online must be able to say.

questions: what is an internet resource locator
what is the difference between a locator and a name
subtitle: The minimum list of properties a resource address must have to work across the whole Internet.

tldr.problem: Information providers and client software need a common way to say where a resource is and how to reach it, or open, widely distributed access on the Internet would be difficult if not impossible.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out nine requirements that narrow a general resource locator down to an Internet locator: transient, global in scope, parsable, distinguishable, transport-friendly, human transcribable, a service plus an opaque parameter package, extensible, and limited to access information.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. It is a checklist for the resource location standards that define the concrete locator formats.

today: RFC 1736 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets requirements for resource location standards rather than defining a locator format itself.

sections.title: What a Resource Locator Is
sections.content:
RFC 1736 specifies a minimum set of requirements for Internet resource locators, which convey location and access information for resources. Typical resources are network accessible documents, WAIS databases, FTP servers and Telnet destinations. Locators may also apply to resources that are not always or not ever network accessible, such as people or physical objects.

A locator is one kind of resource identifier. Other kinds give a resource a name (a stable handle that outlives the resource's location) or a description (meta-information for search and selection). Mapping between these kinds is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: A locator is like the directions to a place. A name says who something is, and a description says what it is like. This memo is only about the directions.

sections.title: The General Locator, Producers and Interpreters
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a deliberately broad definition: a general resource locator is an object that describes the location of a resource. The object could be a byte sequence, a pair of latitude-longitude coordinates or a printed road map. A locator describes a location but never guarantees that access can be established, because the resource may have moved, may be gone, or may not exist yet.

Locators are produced and interpreted. Producers (providers, client software that translates foreign locators, automated databases such as Archie, and users) are bound by the resource location standards, which are in turn bound by these requirements. Interpreters, who may be people or software, are not bound; they benefit from the requirements. A locator may be understood only in part by each of several interpreters, and fully only by a combination of them.

The RFC also lists four senses of "uniqueness" (multiple copies, deterministic access, multiple locators for one resource, and one object per access) and deliberately rejects all of them as requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people write down directions and some people follow them. Directions can be followed in pieces by different helpers, and nobody promises the place is still there.

sections.title: The Nine Requirements
sections.content:
Section 4 applies nine requirements to the general locators, leaving the subset called Internet locators:

  • Transient: the chance that a locator still leads to the resource decreases over time.
  • Global scope: the name space includes the entire world, and success does not depend on where the client is.
  • Parsable: a locator can be broken into complete parts sufficient for an interpreter, human or software, to attempt access.
  • Distinguishable from naming and descriptive identifiers that may share the same name space.
  • Transport-friendly: it can be sent between users, for example by e-mail, without loss or corruption.
  • Human transcribable: it can be copied from voice to paper or paper to keyboard without loss, though not necessarily comfortably.
  • Service plus opaque parameter package: the package has meaning only to the service it is paired with.
  • Extensible: new services can be added over time.
  • Access information only: no type, size or modification date; those belong in resource description standards.

A tenth requirement, that software can reliably recognize locators inside unstructured text such as running ASCII text, was dropped after extensive discussion showed it to be impractical.
sections.plainLanguage: An address must work from anywhere, be easy to read aloud or copy, be able to grow new kinds of places, and say only how to get there, not what is there.

sections.title: Access, Validity and Availability
sections.content:
A locator never guarantees access, but establishing access is by far its most important intended use. The RFC calls it ungracious to advertise a locator for a resource that will never be accessible, yet says it is normal for access to fail at a rate that increases with the age of the locator.

It defines two terms. A locator that conforms to a location standard but fails because the resource was moved, replaced or deleted is invalid; malformed locators are not called invalid. A resource that cannot be reached for predictable reasons, such as certain hours of the day, heavy load or rights clearance restrictions, is unavailable. A locator can be valid and still point to an unavailable resource. Resource naming standards address invalid locators, and resource description standards address some aspects of availability.
sections.plainLanguage: A map can be right even if the shop is closed today or has moved away. Old maps go wrong more often than new ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The requirements have no direct security implications, but applications built on standards that meet them should consider two vulnerabilities. First, because locators are transient, a client using an invalid locator may reach a resource that was not the intended target. For example, a hostname that was unregistered and then re-registered may lead to a resource that only pretends to be the original.

Second, because a locator is a service plus a parameter package, a lot of processing freedom is possible. A server that advertises locators for some local filesystem objects may accidentally expose others unless it restricts its input parameters. A client that trusts a locator from an uncertain source might trigger a mechanism that charges a user account. For services with a lot of user freedom, such as remote login, a locator that pre-specifies commands is risky, and careful command screening can avoid effects such as an embedded rm -fr *.
sections.plainLanguage: An old address might now lead to a stranger's house, and a note that says "do this" should not be followed blindly. Check before you trust it.
